claim: Listen for the low male chant... set over a simple repeating ostinato figure in an irregular metre. (paragraph n17, Halo theme)
problem: The Halo Theme is not in an irregular (asymmetric) metre. Multiple independent musicological sources (Halopedia, published analyses) agree the opening chant section is in 4/4 and the faster string ostinato section that follows is in 12/8 — both are regular metres (simple and compound quadruple respectively), just with a strong triplet feel that can sound unusual on first listen. Calling this 'irregular metre' would lead a student to misdescribe the extract's metre in a listening exam, where this piece sits directly beside the claim as the set embed.
correction: Change to something like: 'set over a simple repeating ostinato figure in a regular but triplet-heavy compound metre (the chant is in 4/4; the faster string ostinato that follows is in 12/8)' — do not describe it as irregular.

claim: Embedded video (id bwikj_lQLT0) captioned: 'Martin O'Donnell - Halo Theme (Halo: Combat Evolved)' — figcaption for the Halo theme figure beside paragraph n16/n17.
problem: The video is titled 'Halo Theme Mjolnir Mix', which is the Halo 2 (2004) remix of the theme (adds two electric guitar parts, performed with Steve Vai) — it is not the original Halo: Combat Evolved (2001) cue. Labelling it '(Halo: Combat Evolved)' misattributes the game, which matters if a student is asked to identify the source game or era from the extract.
correction: Change the figcaption to 'Martin O'Donnell and Michael Salvatori - Halo Theme (Mjolnir Mix, from Halo 2)', or swap the embed for the original Combat Evolved theme if that is what the lesson intends to teach.

claim: Martin O'Donnell's theme for Halo is one of the most famous examples in game music history. (paragraph n16, and repeated through n17)
problem: The Halo Theme was co-composed by Martin O'Donnell AND Michael Salvatori together (both are credited equally on every official soundtrack release and published score). The lesson names O'Donnell only throughout, implying sole authorship. Naming O'Donnell alone is not wrong for a 'name one composer' style question, but the narrative text misleads students about the theme's actual (joint) authorship.
correction: Credit both composers at first mention, e.g. 'Martin O'Donnell and Michael Salvatori's theme for Halo...', while still allowing O'Donnell alone as an acceptable single-composer answer in questions.

claim: ...answered by full orchestra and timpani in a triumphant C major chord. (paragraph n9, Also sprach Zarathustra opening)
problem: The full-orchestra response to the opening trumpet fanfare is not a single triumphant C major chord. It is the piece's famous deliberately ambiguous alternation between a C major chord and a C minor chord (a sixteenth-note apart, with timpani reinforcing both with C-G triplets) — this major/minor clash is the celebrated 'World Riddle' bitonality that is the opening's single most distinctive harmonic feature. Flattening it to 'a triumphant C major chord' removes the one detail most likely to be tested or worth top-band credit in a description of this extract.
correction: Change to describe the ambiguous major/minor alternation, e.g. 'answered by full orchestra and timpani in a famously ambiguous chord that shifts between C major and C minor.'
